cards.explanation: The answer is getting circumcised by the custom of Moses. The men from Judea tell the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” (Acts 15:1) One sentence, friends, and look at the council it sets off. I've seen small things stir up a big mess, but that one is the champion.

The answer is Jerusalem. Paul, Barnabas and some other believers are appointed to go up there to see the apostles and elders about this question (Acts 15:2). They aren't going alone, either. They're sent as a group. When a question gets this big, it helps to bring it to the leaders instead of arguing in the hallway all week.

The answer is joy, and a lot of it. As Paul and Barnabas pass through Phoenicia and Samaria, they recount the conversion of the Gentiles, bringing “…great joy to all the brothers.” (Acts 15:3) That's the news they carried, and joy is what it brought. I think those brothers were smiling long after the visitors left.

The answer is True. Some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.” (Acts 15:5) They say it out loud, in front of everybody. Now the council has a real question on its table.

The word is believe. Peter, one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Luke 6:13-14), says God made a choice that the Gentiles would hear the message of the gospel from his lips “and believe.” (Acts 15:7) He's reminding the room of something God already did. It's hard to argue with what God already did.

The answer is that God gave them the Holy Spirit. Peter says God, who knows the heart, showed His approval “…by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us.” (Acts 15:8) Notice the words just as He did to us. God gave the same gift to both groups. I wouldn't argue with that kind of proof.

The answer is faith, friends. Peter says God “…made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith.” (Acts 15:9) No distinction means no first-class line and second-class line. Same God, same cleansing, same way in.

The answer is False. Peter calls it “…a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10) He says it about himself and the other Jewish believers, and about their fathers too. So they have not been able to bear it.

The answer is through the grace of the Lord Jesus. Peter says, “…we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.” (Acts 15:11) Just as they are. Jewish believers and Gentiles, saved the same way. Peter wraps up his whole speech in one sentence.

The answer is the signs and wonders God did among the Gentiles. The whole assembly fell silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul “…describing the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.” (Acts 15:12) Notice who gets the credit in that sentence. God did them, through Barnabas and Paul. Those two didn't take the credit, and I like that.

The answer is the words of the prophets. James, the one who speaks after Barnabas and Paul finish, says, “The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written…” (Acts 15:15) He doesn't only lean on what Peter said. He brings in what is written. Now there's testimony and Scripture on the same page.

The answer is the remnant of men and all the Gentiles. The quote says, “…so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name…” (Acts 15:17) The Gentiles are right there in the words of the prophet. James picked a good verse for the room.

The answer is False. James says, “…we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God.” (Acts 15:19) He doesn't ask for the whole law of Moses. He says not to cause trouble for the ones turning to God. That's his judgment, friends, and the story keeps going from there.

The answer is sexual immorality. James says to abstain “…from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.” (Acts 15:20) Compare that to the law of Moses that some believers from the party of the Pharisees wanted the Gentiles to obey (Acts 15:5), and it's a short list. Sexual immorality is right there on it.

The answer is Silas. The text says they chose “…Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers…” (Acts 15:22) They send leaders, not just messengers. The whole church is behind this decision, and these two carry it to Antioch.

The answer is False. The letter says, “…some went out from us without our authorization and unsettled you, troubling your minds by what they said.” (Acts 15:24) So the leaders say those men went out without their authorization. They weren't sent by the apostles and elders.

The answer is to tell them in person what the letter says. The letter says, “Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas to tell you in person the same things we are writing.” (Acts 15:27) So the message comes two ways, on paper and by voice. That's some good backup, friends.

The answer is the Holy Spirit. The letter says, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements…” (Acts 15:28) The Holy Spirit is named first in that sentence. The apostles and elders stand right beside Him as the ones it seemed good to.

The answer is True. The text says, “When the people read it, they rejoiced at its encouraging message.” (Acts 15:31) After the sharp debate and the long road, that's a happy ending for the letter. Real encouragement is a gift, friends. They got it in writing.

The answer is prophets. The text says Judas and Silas, “…who themselves were prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers.” (Acts 15:32) They didn't only hand over the letter. They stayed and talked, and the brothers were encouraged and strengthened. Messengers who bring the news and then bring some heart with it are a gift.
